### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Open on the locked-room: Aldo arrives at Crane Manor, examines the sealed study and the body, sets the puzzle (locked deadbolt, latched window, watch stopped at 9:07, wax flake, machine-oil smell). Introduce characters and simmering motive threads (Henry's grief, Marta's protectiveness, Derek's odd presence next door). Plant the clues that will matter later.
Present: char-aldo, char-evelyn, char-henry, char-marta, char-derek, insp-rao, loc-crane, loc-study, obj-study-door, obj-study-window, obj-watch, obj-note, obj-ashtray, obj-wax
Target length: about 700 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

When a well-locked study yields Evelyn Crane's body and a stopped pocket watch, detective-narrator Aldo March must unpick a mechanical trick, a neighbour's machine-smithing, and a ledger of motives to prove a murder that was meant to look impossible.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-aldo: Aldo March — first-person narrator and private investigator in his late thirties, dry, observant, morally impatient; intelligent but not infallible.
- char-evelyn: Evelyn Crane — the victim, a forthright, solitary woman in her fifties who collected antiques and kept meticulous ledgers.
- char-henry: Henry Crane — Evelyn's husband, a reserved retired engineer with a brittle temper and a plausible public grief.
- char-marta: Marta Reyes — long-serving housekeeper to the Cranes, practical, protective of the household and quick with a sharp observation.
- char-derek: Derek Lyle — next-door neighbor, an inventive clock- and small-machinery maker who repairs radiators and makes odd brass contraptions in his shed.
- insp-rao: Inspector Rao — official investigating officer, procedural, careful to keep the record straight, sceptical of private detectives but cooperative.
- loc-crane: Crane Manor — an old three-storey town house with stiff carpets, a coal cellar and a warren of service passages.
- loc-study: The study — Evelyn's locked room on the ground floor: heavy oak door with inside deadbolt, tall fireplace, sash window, low strip of floor near the mantel that conceals a narrow cavity.
- loc-garden: The narrow rear garden between the Cranes' house and Derek's shed; grass, an old coal chute hatch, and a low boundary wall.
- loc-cellar: Coal cellar and service void beneath the study — cramped, coal-smeared, with access from the garden via an old hatch used for deliveries.
- obj-study-door: Heavy oak door of the study fitted with an interior deadbolt and an old brass escutcheon; locked from the inside when the body was found.
- obj-study-window: Sash window in the study, latched and showing no signs of external tampering; the sill bears faint gardener's pollen.
- obj-watch: An engraved antique pocket watch found beneath Evelyn's hand; its hands stopped at 9:07 and its case bears a hairline puncture and faint oil residue.
- obj-note: A small folded scrap of paper clenched in Evelyn's fingers with a two-line cipher and, on the outside, a trace of red sealing-wax.
- obj-ashtray: A crystal ashtray on the desk holding three cigarette butts of an uncommon coarse brand not usually smoked in the house.
- obj-wax: A small flake of red sealing-wax found near the mantel; it matches the residue on the note and the crate-seal impression on a label later found in Derek's shed.
- obj-clockwork: A small clockwork mechanism — brass plates, a wound mainspring and a cam-mounted push-rod — discovered hidden under the hearth; stained with the same oil as the watch.
- obj-ladder: A lightweight aluminium extension ladder leaning against the boundary wall in the garden the morning after the murder; one rung has fresh scraping consistent with being used to reach the coal-hatch.
- obj-coal-hatch: The external coal chute hatch in the garden leading to the cellar beneath the study; its bolt shows recent abrasion and coal dust on the latch.
- obj-filing-mark: A tiny, distinctive filing nick on a brass plate from the clockwork — a maker's tic that Aldo recognises from Derek's workbench.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural solutions or unexplained actions; the locked-room must be resolved by physical mechanism, misdirection, or human action consistent with the environment.
- All clues relied on in the solution must be introduced to the reader (or the narrator) before the reveal scene and have identifiable provenance.
- Times, locations and physical traces must be internally consistent (the watch's stopped time, hatch abrasions, ladder marks, oil stains and filing nick must align with the clockwork reconstruction).
- Forensic detail may be stylised but must not violate basic plausibility (no instantaneous chemical transformations, no impossible mechanical feats).
- The narrator (Aldo) is a competent, essentially reliable detective; he may withhold interpretation but not facts.
- No later scene may introduce new characters, locations, or significant objects not listed above without explicitly adding them to the index with provenance.

## What the index does not have

The context-builder searched for these and came back empty. Each is something this
scene needs, so each one you leave alone is one you will invent without meaning to.

- **Precise wording and provenance of Henry Crane's public statement to the press the morning of the discovery (if any).** (searched: characters/char-henry/profile.yaml; novel/chapters/ch-01/; continuity/; runtime transcripts; news/ || nothing found)
- **Exact years and background of Marta Reyes' service at Crane Manor (how long she's worked for the Cranes, start date).** (searched: characters/char-marta/profile.yaml; novel/characters; novel/chapters; continuity/ || nothing found)
- **Any prior professional interactions between Aldo March and Inspector Rao (previous cases, acquaintance level).** (searched: characters/char-aldo/profile.yaml; characters/insp-rao; continuity/ || nothing found)
- **The precise text of the two-line cipher on the scrap of paper found in Evelyn's hand, or a transcription if available.** (searched: objects/obj-note.yaml; novel/chapters; evidence/ || nothing found)
- **Detailed physical description of the study's visual appearance (carpets, bookcases, mantel details) beyond the brief sketch in loc-study so the narrator can describe the scene's sensory texture.** (searched: locations/loc-study.yaml; novel/chapters; assets/ || nothing found)

For each: either ask `ask_context_builder` — you have 2 questions and they
cost far less than a repair round — or invent it deliberately and put it in your state

in silently; that is the one move nothing downstream can detect.
Allowance for this scene (opening, position 0.125 of the story): 2 repair round(s), 2 follow-up question(s) for the writer, 1 previous scene(s) of prose in the packet.
Why: opening third: almost nothing has been established yet, so there is little for this scene to contradict and little for the writer to have to look up. The allowance is the smallest in the story — rounds not spent here are what pay for the endgame, where the same round buys much more — but it is two rather than one because every opening scene measured so far used its whole allowance and still committed carrying a defect.
It is a ceiling, not a quota. Spending a repair round on a defect the writer cannot see how to fix buys the same draft again — a finding that survives a rewrite unchanged ends the loop whatever the allowance says.
You have room to be sent back here, so a scene that reaches further is worth the risk. What you cannot do is guess at an established fact; a repair round can fix prose and cannot un-invent canon.
Write scene s-001. Call write_staged_scene with the prose, then propose_state_delta with everything it established.
Your packet is also at .context-builder/history/ch-01/s-001.md. If you ask a follow-up, the answer is appended there — read_context re-reads it.

You cannot see the manuscript, so this is the only place that number reaches you — if the book is running short of its target, this scene is where that gets corrected, and a scene that comes in well under its own target is how a book ends up short.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Write the scene in first-person voice, Aldo March. Use the context packet as source. Do not invent new entities. The scene must include each of these facts with provenance as given: door deadbolted from inside, sash window latched, watch under Evelyn's hand stopped at 9:07 with hairline puncture and oil residue, scrap of paper in her fingers sealed with red wax, crystal ashtray with three coarse butts, a flake of wax near the mantel, and the smell of machine oil in the hearth area. Keep the tone dry, observant, and slightly weary. The scene should plant motive threads for Henry, Marta, and Derek but not resolve anything. Target ~700 words. Note: the context-builder flagged gaps for Henry's exact public statement, Marta's years of service, prior interactions between Aldo and Rao, the exact cipher text, and the study's visual micro-description — do not invent those specifics; mention them as gaps or questions Aldo notices he lacks rather than filling them.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

arguments.prose:
People had already gathered inside the study when I arrived: a knot of uniforms and two others who would not leave the picture. Henry stood in the doorway with his shoulders tight as if someone had wound him up and left him running; Marta hovered near the desk, hands folded, protective in the way domestic muscle learns to be. Derek, from next door, lingered in the hall—an odd presence, a man used to measuring things—and Inspector Rao kept to the edge of the room with his notebook open and his face deliberately neutral.

The study itself was obediently quiet. The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill bore faint gardener's pollen. Light pooled on the worn rug and threw the book spines into a dull, anonymous order. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. Beside the blotter a small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three cigarette butts of an uncommon coarse brand not usually smoked in the house. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like something wound too tightly and then let go. I made a point of breathing around it; smells have a way of telling the order of events better than people do.

Those are the hard things you notice and then have to explain: how a room is closed, what was in someone's hand, what the clock on a body says. But there were softer, equally important gaps: I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those gaps matter because motive is a ledger kept in the negative spaces as often as the positive ones. Henry's grief read public and brittle; he sat like a man holding a shape he was trying to make fit. Marta's protectiveness showed in the way she interrupted anyone who moved toward the desk, her voice low and immediate. Derek's presence was odd; he kept to the doorway as if waiting for permission to be useful.

Inspector Rao and I traded the necessary courtesies and left the room in each other's hands—his in the legal sense, mine more practical. The study would be sealed again and logged; evidence would be photographed and catalogued. For now, the scene had done its work: it had given me a lock slid from the inside, a latched window, a stopped watch with a tiny wound, wax on paper and fireplace, a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place butts, and the smell of machines in the hearth. It had also left me with questions I could not yet answer.

That, in the end, is what a locked room asks of you: not simply the obvious impossibility but the list of things you do not yet know. I pencilled them into my notebook and closed it on the study's edge; someone else would run the photographs, but I was the one who had to begin the ledger.

The packet is your source of *facts*, never of *sentences*. If that came from an entity file, it is registry language: it exists to record what is true, and it reads as an index dump on the page. A measured run put two object-file lines in quotation marks in its opening paragraphs and scored the lowest reading-experience mark this system has recorded. If it came from an earlier scene's prose, that is restatement, which the graders penalise in a long story for good reason. Say the same fact in your own narration and call this again.

arguments.prose:
People had gathered before I stepped over the threshold: a pair of uniforms doing their polite, slow circuit, Henry Crane standing as if he were a model of restraint, Marta planted like a hinge beside the desk, Derek from next door lingering in the hall with the careful stillness of a man who watches mechanisms, and Inspector Rao keeping to the edge with his notebook closed but ready.

The heavy oak door's deadbolt had been slid from the inside. The sash window was latched; the sill showed a faint dusting of garden pollen. Light lay across the floorboards in a flat, indifferent pool. Evelyn lay where she had fallen, half-turned toward the fireplace; her fingers were clenched around a small, stubborn thing.

Her hand still clutched an engraved pocket watch; its hands had stopped at 9:07, and the case bore a hairline puncture and a faint film of oil. A small folded scrap of paper was clenched in her fingers, sealed with a trace of red sealing-wax. On the desk a crystal ashtray held three short, rough-ended butts of a coarse tobacco I did not recognise from the household's usual brand. Near the mantel I found a small flake of red sealing-wax.

There was the smell of machine oil about the hearth—sharp and metallic in the air, like a lathe left running and then abandoned. It sat in the room as insistently as any witness.

Those are the things the room offers first: how it was closed, what was in a body's hold, what time a stopped instrument insists upon. But there were other absences I noticed at once. I had not seen any precise wording of Henry Crane's statement to the press. There was no record I could find of how long Marta Reyes had worked here. I couldn't tell from the material in my hands whether Rao and I had ever met before. The scrap bore a two-line cipher; I had not been given a transcription of its exact letters. What I lacked was a close, micro-description of the study's carpets and mantel—those small details the inventory summary overlooks.

Those absences matter. Henry's grief read public and sharp; he held himself with the taut courtesy of someone who thinks performance protects feeling. Marta moved around the desk as if its surface were hers to defend: a hand on a corner of the blotter, a look that dared anyone to reach for the watch. Derek's presence was a different note—he lingered like a neighbour who knows the machinery of houses and notices when a machine smells wrong.

Rao and I exchanged the professional gestures required of men who are to be expected to work together: a nod, a brief mention that evidence would be photographed and the scene logged. The study would be sealed again. For now, there was only the list: a deadbolt slid from the inside; a latched sash window; a stopped watch beneath a dead woman's hand reading 9:07 with a puncture and oil on its case; wax on the note and a flake by the mantel; a crystal ashtray with three out-of-place cigarette butts; the smell of machine oil at the hearth. And the gaps—the things I could not yet put in my ledger.

I made notes. Photographing and cataloguing are someone else's ordinance; deduction is mine. A locked room is a contract that begins with a set of physical sentences and leaves you to supply the connecting verbs. I closed my notebook on that edge and let the room keep its silence a little longer—waiting is part of listening.
